_doc: HAND-AUTHORED for T-0567. The DATED TOWN FINDINGS of Norris's 1844 directory — the Description and Historical Sketch (scan leaves 15-30 = printed pages 5-20) and the Statistical Account (leaves 76-88 = printed 66-78), which are the two parts of the volume that are prose and tables rather than a list of names, and which T-0566 deliberately did not read. Every claim is `town_finding: true`: a statement ABOUT THE TOWN, not about a person's address. Every quote is lifted unedited out of the committed page text and is rebuilt character-for-character by tools/research_domains.py --check, which is this file's gate; the OCR damage is left in on purpose, and the repair is in `normalized`. THE FIELD THAT MATTERS IS `describes_date`: it is the year the STATEMENT describes and not 1844, so the handful of sentences in which Norris speaks about the scene year of this reconstruction are separable from the ninety per cent that are not. Nothing here has been written into a resident, household, business or structure record. Under the ratified ladder of 2026-09-03 a source printed nine years after the scene never on its own makes an 1835 fact; T-0569 is the ticket that spends this on the layers.
reading_note: transcription_mediated throughout, for the same reason the 2,073 directory entries are: this is archive.org's OCR of the printed page and it has not been checked against the image by eye. Three OCR slips in this file change a DATE and are called out in the notes of the claims that carry them — '1932' for 1832 (leaf 16), '1617' for 1816 (leaf 21) and '1342' for 1842 (leaf 27). Each is repaired only in `normalized`; the quote keeps the damage so it can be found on the page again.

claims.quote:
site of the City occupies a level prairie, on both sides of the majn
stream, and the North and South Branches of Chicago River, and
covers an area of about three and a half miles in length. North arid
South, and two and a half in breadth, East and West, about a mile
and a half square of which is already regularly built upon, and the
streets opened and graded. The streets are regularly laid out, pa-
claims.normalized: Norris describes the city site as a level prairie on both sides of the main stream and the North and South Branches, about 3.5 miles north-south by 2.5 east-west, of which about a mile and a half square was regularly built upon and its streets opened and graded — the built extent of 1844, nine years after the scene.
claims.notes: The GRID and the built extent. For 1835 this is a ceiling, not a measurement: a mile and a half square built up in 1844 is more than 1835 had, and the sketch says so itself on leaf 21. Filed as the 1844 statement it is.

claims.quote:
streets opened and graded. The streets are regularly laid out, pa-
  rallel and at right angles to the Lake, and are wide and spacious.
claims.normalized: The streets are laid out parallel and at right angles to the lake, and are wide and spacious.
claims.notes: Corroborates the orientation of the plat this reconstruction builds on — the 1830 canal-commissioners' grid squared to the lake, not to true north. It is an 1844 statement about a grid laid out in 1830 and unchanged, which is why it is worth having.

claims.quote:
There are several extensive blocks of brick buildings, principally
occupied as business houses and public offices, three and a half and
four stories in height. The dwellings are principally of wood,
many of them, however, very fine specimens of correct architecture.
claims.normalized: By 1844 there were several extensive blocks of brick buildings three and a half to four storeys high, occupied mainly as business houses and public offices, while the dwellings were principally of wood.
claims.notes: NOT an 1835 fact and the contrast is the point: brick blocks three and four storeys high are the town of 1844. Leaf 22 dates the FIRST brick buildings to 1834. What carries back is the proportion — dwellings principally of wood — which the reconstruction already builds to.

claims.quote:
The portion of the City extending several miles along the shore of
the Lake, is sandy, and consequently at all seasons, dry. The por-
  tion removed from the Lake partakes of the character of all level
prairie, Itoing in the spring and fall wet and muddy. The site of the
claims.normalized: The lakeward strip of the city is sandy and dry at all seasons; the portion away from the lake is level prairie and is wet and muddy in spring and fall.
claims.notes: A ground-condition statement that does carry back, because it is about the soil and not about the buildings: the sand ridge along the shore against the wet prairie behind it. Relevant to the terrain and to how the streets read underfoot.

claims.quote:
rounding country, a very interesting field of vision. Chicago River
and its branches, which run through the heart of the City, and ad-
  mit at nil seasons, vessels of every class, navigating the Lake, some
distance into the interior, afford peculiar facilities for a harbor, and
claims.normalized: Chicago River and its branches run through the heart of the city and admit vessels of every class navigating the lake some distance into the interior, which is what gives the place its harbour.
claims.notes: The river as the harbour. The pier works that made the entrance passable are dated on leaf 23 to late 1833; this is the 1844 statement of what the river itself does.

claims.quote:
an incorporated City, the act of the legislature conferring its charter
being granted and approved March 4th of that year. The City is
divided into six Wards. The first and second Wards, divided by
claims.normalized: Chicago became an incorporated city by an act of the legislature granted and approved 4 March 1837, and was divided into six wards.
claims.notes: AFTER the scene. In 1835 Chicago was an incorporated TOWN, not a city, and had no six wards. Filed because the ward boundaries Norris then gives are the frame every later list in this volume — including the 1843 census on leaf 86 — is counted in, and a reader who takes those wards back to 1835 is making a mistake this claim names.

claims.quote:
divided into six Wards. The first and second Wards, divided by
Clark Street, are bounded by the South Branch-, Chicago River, and
the Lake—the first Ward lying East, and the second West of Clark
Street. The third and fourth Wards, divided by Randolph Street,
are situated on the West side of the North and South Branches—
the third South, and the fourth North of Randolph Street. The
fifth and sfxth Wards, divided by Clark Street, are bounded by the
North Branch, Chicago River, and the Lake—the fifth being West,
and the sixth East of Clark Street. The government of the City is
claims.normalized: The six wards of 1844: first and second divided by Clark Street between the South Branch, the river and the lake (first east, second west); third and fourth divided by Randolph Street on the west side of the branches (third south, fourth north); fifth and sixth divided by Clark Street between the North Branch, the river and the lake (fifth west, sixth east).
claims.notes: The key to every ward-counted table in this volume, the 1843 census on leaf 86 above all. It is 1844 geography and must not be read back to 1835.

claims.quote:
1932, and the beginning of 1833, Chicago had about 100 inhabitants
and five or six log houses, exclusive of the Fort and its appurte-
claims.normalized: In 1832 and the beginning of 1833 Chicago had about 100 inhabitants and five or six log houses, exclusive of the fort and its appurtenances. (The printed '1932' is an OCR slip for 1832; the same statement is made again in the sketch's own words on leaf 21.)
claims.notes: ONE OF THE TWO NUMBERS IN THIS BOOK THAT BEAR DIRECTLY ON THE RECONSTRUCTION'S PROBLEM — what the town was immediately before it grew. Norris repeats it on leaf 21 ('some five or six houses, built mostly of logs, and a population of less than one hundred') and names those houses one by one on leaf 22, which is the passage worth having. Written nine years later and not a census.

claims.quote:
nances. In 1840, the population had increased to 4853. The pre-
  sent population exceeds 7580, and may be said at this time to amount
to 8000. The period of the greatest prosperity of Chicago, was
claims.normalized: The 1840 population was 4,853; the population when Norris wrote exceeded 7,580 and could be said to amount to 8,000.
claims.notes: The 7,580 is S. W. Norris's own census of 1 August 1843, tabulated on leaf 86. The 4,853 is the federal census of 1840, which is the deposit the census_1840 domain is reading. Neither is 1835; the 1835 figure Norris gives is on leaf 23.

claims.quote:
to 8000. The period of the greatest prosperity of Chicago, was
from 1833 to 1837. The revulsions and reverses of '3G-7, greatly
•retarded its growth. It continued, however, though more gradually,
to increase in business and resources until 1840-1, from which tim«
business received a new impulse, and it is now enjoying a degree of
prosperity equal to any former period of ks history.
claims.normalized: The period of Chicago's greatest prosperity was from 1833 to 1837; the reverses of 1836-7 retarded its growth, which continued more gradually until 1840-1, from which time business received a new impulse.
claims.notes: Puts the scene year of this reconstruction — 1835 — inside the boom, and dates the boom's ends. Norris's periodisation, not a measurement.

claims.quote:
"We behold it, from a distant arid isolated colony, inhabited only by
some five or six families clineing to a lone and solitary military
post for protection, and dependent for subsistence upon t-be uncer-
  tain arrival of some chance vessel from Mackinaw, in the short sprrce
claims.normalized: Norris's summary of the beginning: an isolated colony inhabited only by some five or six families clinging to a lone military post for protection, dependent for subsistence on the uncertain arrival of a chance vessel from Mackinaw, which became a city in the space of eight or ten years.
claims.notes: Rhetoric, and filed as such — but it repeats the five-or-six-families figure a third time, and it dates the transformation to 'eight or ten years' before 1844, which brackets 1834-1836. `describes_date` is set to the earliest year the span can mean.

claims.quote:
The original proprietors and first inhabitants of the region, were, of
course, the aborigines. The description of the first appearance of
the vicinity, by some of its earliest explorers, leads to the belief, that
they were here from a very early period; that this was, then, and
from time immemorial had been, the site of an Indian village.
claims.normalized: Norris holds that the site was an Indian village from a very early period, citing the number and apparent antiquity of the trails centring here as reported by Major Long.
claims.notes: The TRAILS are the part that touches this reconstruction: the routes converging on the portage are older than the plat and some of them survive in the 1830s roads. Norris is reporting Long, not observing. `describes_date` is set to the earliest event the passage anchors, the first documented visit he goes on to date.

claims.quote:
The French wore the original discoverers and settlers of the West.
As parly ns the latter part of the. sixteenth century, while (he Eng-
  lish Colonies were yet clinging to the shores of tlie Atlantic, almost
two hundred years ago, the,ir voyages and expeditions to this region
commenced. In a few years they discovered, and to some extent,
settled the uliole vnst region from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico,
claims.normalized: The French were the original discoverers and settlers of the West, their voyages to this region beginning in the latter part of the sixteenth century.
claims.notes: Background, and Norris's century is wrong — Marquette is 1673, which he dates correctly on leaf 18. Filed so that leaf 17 is reached and so the error is on the record rather than tidied out.

claims.quote:
reaping the fruits of all their toils and sufferings. The earliest of
these expeditions, as well as the most distinguished, were those of
Marquette and La Salle. The former occurred in the year 1673,
and resulted in the discovery of the Mississippi, the original object
and design of the expedition. To this expedition, is probably to be
ascribed the honor of paying the first visit to Chicago, it being the
prevailing opinion that it passed through here on its return to
Canada, ascending the Illinois River and crossing to Michigan.
claims.normalized: Marquette's expedition of 1673 discovered the Mississippi, and Norris takes the prevailing opinion to be that it passed through Chicago on its return to Canada, ascending the Illinois River and crossing to Michigan — probably the first visit to the site.
claims.notes: Pre-history of the site, filed as a dated claim rather than a fact: Norris himself says 'it being the prevailing opinion', which is the grade of the statement.

claims.quote:
On the third day of August, 1795, at the treaty held by General
Wayne, with the Pottawatamies and other tribes at Greenville, the
title to six miles square of territory, at the mouth of Chikajo River,
as it is expressed in the treaty, was obtained' by the United States.
claims.normalized: At the Treaty of Greenville, 3 August 1795, the United States obtained title to six miles square at the mouth of the Chicago River.
claims.notes: The land title under the whole town. Dated and specific, and it is the cession the 1830 plat is eventually laid out inside.

claims.quote:
had made a settlement here, many years before. In 1804, Fort
Chicago was built on the site of the present Fort. About the same
time, the American Fur Company, having been organised shortly
before, established a trading station, under the protection of the
Garrison. The little colony thus planted here, some forty years ago,
for military and trading purposes, may- be regarded as the first at-
claims.normalized: Fort Chicago was built in 1804 on the site of the fort standing in 1844, and about the same time the American Fur Company established a trading station under the protection of the garrison — which Norris calls the first attempt at a permanent settlement.
claims.notes: DATES THE FUR COMPANY POST, which is one of the buildings this reconstruction holds. Norris puts the 1804 fort on the same site as the later one; the fort standing in 1835 is the 1816 rebuild, dated on leaf 21.

claims.quote:
what in detail, in this connection. Beside the Garrison, there were
several families residing here at the time. Mr. John Kinzie, father
of John H. Kin/.ie, Esq., present Register of the Land Office in this
City, occupied a house on the North side of the River, a little East
of the present site of the Lake House. The evacuation took place
claims.normalized: In August 1812 several families besides the garrison lived here, and John Kinzie — father of John H. Kinzie, in 1844 Register of the Land Office — occupied a house on the north side of the river, a little east of the site of the Lake House.
claims.notes: LOCATES THE KINZIE HOUSE by a landmark still standing in 1844, and does it twice (leaf 22 repeats it). The Kinzie house is a structure this reconstruction has to place, and 'a little East of the present site of the Lake House' is the most usable locator in the sketch. It is a recollection of 1812 written in 1844, not a survey.

claims.quote:
ted to the Indians. Under these circumstances, about nine o'clock,
on the morning of the 15th of August, the party, composed of 54
regulars, 12 militia, and several families, amounting in nil to about
70 persons, left the Fort, under the escort of Capt. Wells, and about
30 Miami Indians. Their route lay along the beach of the LaK-e,
between the water on the left, and a succession of sand hills on the
right. They had proceeded about a mile and a half from the Fort,
claims.normalized: About nine on the morning of 15 August 1812 a party of 54 regulars, 12 militia and several families — about 70 persons in all — left the fort escorted by Captain Wells and about 30 Miami, along the lake beach, and was attacked about a mile and a half from the fort.
claims.notes: The evacuation and the battle. Outside the scene by 23 years, but it is the event that makes the fort standing in 1835 a REBUILD, and Norris's figures here are his own count from an eye-witness.

claims.quote:
to, and the arms delivered up. The survivors were marched back
to the Indian encampment, near the Fort, about the spot where
State Street now opens to'the River, and where the present Market
claims.normalized: The survivors were marched back to the Indian encampment near the fort, about the spot where State Street opened to the river and where the market stood in 1844.
claims.notes: An 1812 place fixed by an 1844 street. Useful only as a locator, and the street it names did not exist under that name in 1812.

claims.quote:
The Fort was rebuilt in 1617, when it took the name of Fort
Dearborn. It was occupied, except at short intervals, by a Gar-
  rison, until 1837, when, the Indians having generally left the coun-
  try, it was finally evacuated, and has never since been re-occupied
as a military post. It remains in much the same condition as in
claims.normalized: The fort was rebuilt in 1816 — the printed '1617' is an OCR slip — took the name Fort Dearborn, and was occupied by a garrison, except at short intervals, until 1837, when it was finally evacuated and never re-occupied as a military post.
claims.notes: THE FORT STANDING IN THE SCENE. 1835 falls inside the occupied span this sentence gives, so Norris corroborates a garrisoned Fort Dearborn at the scene date. The 1617 is unmistakably 1816 and the repair is in `normalized` only, per this domain's rule.

claims.quote:
as a military post. It remains in much the same condition as in
'37, except the pnllisadcs, which were removed, the past spring, and
their place supplied by a handsome fence. It has since been occu-
claims.normalized: In 1844 the fort remained in much the same condition as in 1837 except that the palisades had been removed the past spring and replaced by a fence.
claims.notes: Dates the REMOVAL of the palisades to spring 1844 — which is to say the palisades were standing through the scene year and for nine years after it. A negative-evidence statement of real value to a reconstruction that has to decide whether to build them.

claims.quote:
bandry, or pasturage. So late as '35 or '6, the fires usual on the
prairies in the fall, overran the third and fourth wards. There were
only some five or six houses, built mostly of logs, and a population
of less than one hundred.
claims.normalized: As late as 1835 or 1836 the usual autumn prairie fires overran the third and fourth wards; there were only some five or six houses, mostly of logs, and a population of less than one hundred.
claims.notes: READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. The prairie-fire half is a SCENE-YEAR statement and is the only sentence in the sketch that describes the ground in 1835 or 1836: fire ran over what became the third and fourth wards, west of the branches. The house-count half is NOT about 1835 — the paragraph is describing 1832, Norris has already given the same figures for 1832 twice, and the town of 1835 had hundreds of buildings by every other source this project holds. The sentence is filed whole and unedited because that is the rule, and the split is stated here so no later pass reads five or six houses as an 1835 fact.

claims.quote:
One of the^e houses, formerly the property of the Fur Company,
was, until a short time past, occupied by Col. Beaubien. About 80
rods to the south of that, stood a house, once occupied by Colonel
Owings, but since washed away by the Lake. A house, known as
"Cobweb Castle," on block No. 1, was formerly the abode of Dr.
Alexander Wolcott.
claims.normalized: Of the houses standing in 1832: one, formerly the Fur Company's, was occupied until shortly before 1844 by Col. Beaubien; about 80 rods south of it stood a house once occupied by Colonel Owings, since washed away by the lake; and 'Cobweb Castle' on block No. 1 was formerly the abode of Dr. Alexander Wolcott.
claims.notes: THE MOST USEFUL PASSAGE IN THE SKETCH FOR THIS PROJECT and the reason T-0567 is worth a run. Three named buildings with occupants and two with locations — the Fur Company house Beaubien took, Owings's house 80 rods (about 1,320 feet) south of it, and Wolcott's Cobweb Castle on block 1. All three are 1832 buildings; whether they still stood on 1 July 1835 is a separate question this claim does not answer. Owings's is recorded as lost to the lake by 1844.

claims.quote:
The dwelling of Mr. John Kinzie stood East^f the Lake House.
A log building at the corner of Dearborn and South Water Streets,
and the once celebrated tavern of Mr. Mark Beaubien, on the site
of the Sauganash. generally known as the Eagle, together with a
building on block 14, and a cabin, occupied by. Robinson, the In-
  dian Chief at Wolf Point, constituted all the buildings, except the
Fort, to be found here in 1832. Sometime this year, however,
claims.normalized: Norris's inventory of what stood at Chicago in 1832, besides the fort: John Kinzie's dwelling east of the Lake House; a log building at the corner of Dearborn and South Water Streets; Mark Beaubien's tavern on the site of the Sauganash, known as the Eagle; a building on block 14; and a cabin at Wolf Point occupied by Robinson, the Indian chief.
claims.notes: A NAMED, LOCATED INVENTORY of the pre-boom town — five buildings, four of them with a street, block or landmark. Every one of them is a candidate identification for a structure this reconstruction places, and the corner of Dearborn and South Water and 'block 14' are locators the plat can take directly. 1832, not 1835: what this fixes is the floor the scene was built up from.

claims.quote:
Fort, to be found here in 1832. Sometime this year, however,
Kobert A. Kinzie built a store at Wolf Point, the first frame build-
  ing in Chicago. la 1834, several brick buildings were erected.
claims.normalized: Robert A. Kinzie built a store at Wolf Point sometime in 1832 — the first frame building in Chicago — and in 1834 several brick buildings were erected.
claims.notes: TWO DATED FIRSTS, both before the scene. The first frame building (1832, Wolf Point, R. A. Kinzie) and the first brick (1834, unnamed). Both bear on what materials the town of 1 July 1835 could plausibly show, and the brick date is the one that matters: brick was one year old in the scene.

claims.quote:
The commerce of the place, up to this period, was equally insig-
  nificant. In fact, there was none, unless the traffic of the Fur Com-
  pany, can be dignified with that name. Vessels occasionally ven-
  tured here, but so seldom, that the arrival of a schooner was an
event of no little moment, and created a sensation throughout the
cotpraunity. The year 1832, may then be regarded as the period
from which to date the commencement of the City. Many causes,
claims.normalized: Commerce before 1832 was insignificant — none, Norris says, but the Fur Company's traffic. Vessels came so seldom that the arrival of a schooner was an event. He dates the commencement of the city to 1832.
claims.notes: The trade baseline the scene year grew out of, and the American Fur Company's standing in it. T-0575 reads Hurlbut on the same trade.

claims.quote:
The attention of Congress had been called to the importance and
necessity of a harbor, and an appropriation was confidently relied
upon at the next session. Gen. Scott, who explored Hie country
during the Indian war, took a lively interest in this work, and ad-
  dressed a letter in relation to it, which was subsequently laid be-
claims.normalized: Congress had been called to the necessity of a harbour and an appropriation was relied on; General Scott, who explored the country during the Indian war, took an interest and addressed a letter on it that was laid before Congress.
claims.notes: The harbour appropriation that produced the piers whose construction leaf 23 dates to late 1833 — the works standing, half-built, in the scene.

claims.quote:
ment projected. The sale of Canal lots in 1830 hns been already
mentioned. ' In 1833, a great Indian payment was held here, near
the present site of the Lake House. In the latter part of this year,
the work on the harbor was commenced—and during the same year,
the present Light-house was erected, the old one having fallen
claims.normalized: In 1833 a great Indian payment was held near the site of the Lake House; in the latter part of that year work on the harbour was commenced; and during the same year the present light-house was erected, the old one having fallen down.
claims.notes: THREE DATED WORKS, all 1833, all standing or under way in the scene: the harbour work, the light-house (a REPLACEMENT — the earlier one had fallen), and the payment ground near the later Lake House. The light-house is a structure this reconstruction has to decide about, and this dates the one that stood in 1835 to 1833.

claims.quote:
down. In 1835, the population of the place was said to amount to
5,500, a computation which probably included transitory persons, a
great many of whom were here at the time. The actual popula-
  tion, however, that year, could not have been much less than 3000.
claims.normalized: In 1835 the population was said to amount to 5,500, a computation Norris thinks included transitory persons, a great many of whom were here at the time; the actual population that year, he holds, could not have been much less than 3,000.
claims.notes: THE SCENE-YEAR POPULATION, and the single most directly relevant sentence in the volume. Norris gives BOTH the contemporary claim (5,500, inflated by transients) and his own nine-years-later judgement (not much less than 3,000), and the gap between them is exactly the transient question this project's household reconstruction keeps meeting. It is a recollection, not a count: no census of Chicago was taken in 1835. Filed as a claim about 1835, never as the population.

claims.quote:
In 1836, another sale of Canal lots took place, which was attended
with much excitement, and occasioned a large collection of people
from distant quarters. The prices were extravagantly high. In
1836, a branch of the State Bank was located here. On the 4th of
claims.normalized: In 1836 a second sale of canal lots drew a large collection of people from distant quarters at extravagantly high prices, and a branch of the State Bank was located here.
claims.notes: The year AFTER the scene, and it is the year the scene's speculation crested. Bounds the 1835 town from above.

claims.quote:
tators. During the winter of'36-7, the act to incorporate the City,
passed the State Legislature; and in April succeeding, the first elec-
  tion under the Charter was held, which resulted in the choice of
W. B. OODEN to the office of Mayor. The growth cf commerce,
claims.normalized: The act to incorporate the city passed during the winter of 1836-7, and at the first election under the charter, in April 1837, W. B. Ogden was chosen mayor.
claims.notes: After the scene. Filed because Ogden is a name the 1835 layers already carry and this dates his mayoralty, which is not an 1835 office.

claims.quote:
than the accumulation of this world's goods. Before or during
1836, as many as six Churches had been organized, and suitable
buildings provided for their accommodation. ' These Churches,
claims.normalized: Before or during 1836 as many as six churches had been organised and suitable buildings provided for them.
claims.notes: A CEILING ON CHURCHES AT THE SCENE, and a useful one: six church buildings by the end of 1836 means fewer than six in mid-1835. The church domain (T-0503, St Mary's register) is reading the same ground from the registers.

claims.quote:
Neither was the subject of education wholly neglected. The school
section, which fortunately lay contiguous to the City, and was pro-
portionably valuable, was disposed of in 1834, and the avails applied
to the support of Common Schools. Means for the diffusion of
claims.normalized: The school section, lying contiguous to the city, was disposed of in 1834 and the proceeds applied to the support of common schools.
claims.notes: Dates the school-section sale to 1834 — the year before the scene, and the transaction that put a large block of the near south side into private hands. Bears on who owned what in 1835.

claims.quote:
In 1834, John Calhoun commenced the publication of the Chi-
  cago Democrat; and:in the following year, Thos. O. Davis esta-
  blished the Chicago American, both of which papers still exist; the
claims.normalized: John Calhoun commenced publication of the Chicago Democrat in 1834, and in the following year Thomas O. Davis established the Chicago American; both papers still existed in 1844.
claims.notes: DIRECTLY CORROBORATES THIS PROJECT'S OWN NEWSPAPER CORPUS. The Democrat (1834) and the American (1835) are the two papers whose 1835 issues this repository holds and reads; Norris independently dates the founding of both and names their founders.

claims.quote:
latter under the name of the Chicago Express, being published
daily. These papers, together with the Prairie Farmer, Agricultu-
  ral; the Western Citizen, Abolition; the North-Western"Baptist,
Baptist; and the Better Covenant, Universalist, which Intve since
been started,'are ably conducted, and have an extensive circulation.
claims.normalized: By 1844 the American was published daily as the Chicago Express, and the Prairie Farmer (agricultural), the Western Citizen (abolition), the North-Western Baptist and the Better Covenant (Universalist) had since been started.
claims.notes: 1844 press, none of it in the scene. Filed because it says which of the papers this project reads survived and under what name, which is what a later run tracing a citation needs.

claims.quote:
apparent even then. It raged with great violence during '35-6,
and a portion of '37, at which time it gave color and direction to
most business transactions.
claims.normalized: Speculation raged with great violence during 1835-6 and part of 1837, and at that time gave colour and direction to most business transactions.
claims.notes: A SCENE-YEAR STATEMENT ABOUT WHAT THE TOWN WAS DOING. In the summer of 1835 the dominant business of Chicago was, on Norris's account, trading in land. It bears on what the shopfronts and offices of the reconstruction should be.

claims.quote:
themselves. But little was gained during '38-9; but in '40, things
assumed a more favorable aspect, and since that time the increase
of business and population has been most rapid. This will be
claims.normalized: Little was gained in 1838-9, but in 1840 things assumed a more favourable aspect, and since then the increase of business and population had been most rapid.
claims.notes: The recovery, after the scene. Filed to date the trough between the 1835 boom and the town of the directory.

claims.quote:
The principal difficulty encountered during the progress of the
harbor has been occasioned by the deposition of sand and the for-
  mation of bars at its mouth. The plans heretofore adopted to sur-
  mount this difficulty have failed upon trial, and are now abandoned.
Two plans have been proposed the present season, which have at-
  tracted considerable attention. One of these, suggested by Captain
McLellan, the present superintendent, recommends the construc-
  tion of a pier north of the present ones, at a distance from them
greater than the length of the present bar, and is based upon the
supposition that the sand would form a bar around its head, and not
reach the entrance of the harbor. The other plan, which has been
claims.normalized: The chief difficulty at the harbour was the deposition of sand and the formation of bars at its mouth; the plans adopted before 1844 had failed on trial and were abandoned, and Captain McLellan, the superintendent, proposed a pier north of the existing ones beyond the length of the bar.
claims.notes: THE SANDBAR IS THE PERMANENT FACT and it is the one thing about the harbour that certainly holds for 1835: the mouth silted, and every plan tried in the first decade failed. The reconstruction's river mouth has to show a bar.

claims.quote:

It says exactly what arrived at Chicago in 1835 and how often: a four-horse stage, three times a week, carrying the eastern mail. That is a coach in the street, on a schedule, in the summer of 1835 — and it names the postmasters on either side of the scene. `describes_date` is 1835 because that is the year the sequence is filed for; the sentence covers 1832-1837.

claims.normalized: Norris's remark on his own method: the census was taken with great care, all persons not permanently residing in the city being in every instance excluded, and the population could have been made 8,500 by including the transitory persons it is customary to count.

Norris drew a line between permanent and transitory residents and put roughly 900 people on the far side of it — and it is the same line he says the 1835 figure of 5,500 fell on the wrong side of (leaf 23). It is the transient problem, named by a nineteenth-century enumerator, in the source itself.

claims.notes: FILED WITH ITS REFUSAL WRITTEN OUT. Norris prints the 1843 census as a wide ruled table and archive.org's OCR has woven its columns into a single stream — every count on this page has lost the heading that says what it counts. The three nativity ROWS survive as rows and are quoted; THE NUMBERS BESIDE THEM CANNOT BE READ OFF THIS TEXT and are not asserted here. Two totals on the page are unambiguous and are: the whole number of families, 1,177, and the grand totals 4,853 (1840) and 7,580 (1843). Closing the rest needs the page IMAGE, and this claim is the declaration that it has not been closed.

claims.normalized: Chicago's recorded trade by year from the revenue office. EXPORTS: $1,000.64 in 1836, $11,065.00 in 1837, $16,044.75 in 1838, $33,843.00 in 1839, $228,635.74 in 1840, $348,362.24 in 1841, $659,305.20 in 1842. IMPORTS: $325,203.90 in 1836, $373,667.12 in 1837, $579,174.61 in 1838, $630,980.26 in 1839, $562,106.20 in 1840, $564,347.88 in 1841, $664,347.88 in 1842. The OCR floated the IMPORTS heading to the second line of the quote and then set the two tables one after the other; the pairing of year to figure is read off that order and the leading 8 of $325,203.90 is the OCR of a dollar sign.
claims.notes: THE TRADE SERIES STARTS IN 1836, ONE YEAR AFTER THE SCENE, AND STARTS AT A THOUSAND DOLLARS OF EXPORTS AGAINST $325,000 OF IMPORTS. That is the finding: in the year after 1835 Chicago exported a thousand dollars' worth of everything. The town of the scene was an IMPORTING town living off the lake trade and the land office, not a grain port — the grain port is the 1840s. Norris warns on the same page that the figures are below the true amount because vessels left unreported.
